## **M u s s e l r o e W i n d F a r m**

Development Proposal and Environmental Management Plan August 2004

## Supplementary Information Two

Revised Avian Impact Assessment

## **MUSSELROE WIND FARM**

**DEVELOPMENT PROPOSAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN**

**SECOND SUPPLEMENT - REVISED AVIAN IMPACT ASSESSMENT**

HYDRO ELECTRIC CORPORATION ARBN 072 377 158 ABN 48 072 377 158 4 Elizabeth Street, Hobart Tasmania, Australia

Report No: 117116-Report-6 Rev. Status: 0 Date Issued: 23/08/2004

## **FOREWORD**

This document provides additional supplementary information on the Musselroe Wind Farm Development Proposal and Environmental Management Plan (DPEMP) for the purposes of environmental and planning assessment.  Specifically, this document provides information on the revised impact assessment for avifauna following the revision of the collision risk model that has been used to support the avifauna impact assessment.

On 31 March 2003, Hydro Tasmania submitted a Development Application (including the supporting DPEMP) to Dorset Council. The Application is seeking a planning permit to construct and operate a wind farm on the Cape Portland Property adjacent to Little Musselroe Bay on the north-east coast of Tasmania, and to construct and operate a 110 kV transmission line within a corridor of land to connect the Wind Farm to the Tasmanian electricity grid at the Derby Electricity Sub-Station.

In response to comments from the public and government agencies, Hydro Tasmania submitted a Supplement to the DPEMP to Dorset Council in September 2003.

During subsequent assessments, Hydro Tasmania found that the collision risk model used to assess impacts to avifauna in the DPEMP and supplement contained a computational flaw. As a result, the formal assessment process was postponed and Hydro Tasmania and Biosis Research comprehensively reviewed the collision risk model. The computational flaw was corrected and a number of additional refinements were made to the model resulting in a more robust model.

This document provides information on the following:

-  Details of the revision of the deterministic collision risk model;

-  The results of revised avian collision risk modelling and avifauna impact assessment;

-  Revised commitments for mitigation of assessed impacts;

-  The consolidated list commitments for the Project; and

-  Additional supporting documentation.

The results of the revised avian collision risk modelling and changes to the assessed impact to priority species reported in this document replace those reported for priority species in the DPEMP Volume 4, Appendix 3a pp 141-145 and Volume 2, Chapter 7, section 7.3. Proposed mitigation for assessed impacts to priority species, contained in the first Supplement to the DPEMP is revised based on available information.

## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

## **Introduction to modelling**

Hydro Tasmania has a large and comprehensive development strategy for wind farms in Australia, particularly in Tasmania where significant developments are underway (e.g. Woolnorth), or are in the planning stages (e.g. Musselroe, Heemskirk and others).  Two of the three planned stages of the Woolnorth development have been completed, whilst the development approval process for Musselroe and Heemskirk Wind Farms is nearing finalisation.  One of the main environmental issues for wind farm developments to address in the approval phase of the development is the potential impact to avifauna. Whilst it is recognized that all forms of stationary (e.g. communication towers) and moving infrastructure (e.g. vehicles) will have a degree of avifauna mortality associated with its operation, it has been difficult for wind farm proponents in particular to obtain development approvals for projects.

In the absence of empirical data on the impact of wind farms in Australia, one way to provide regulators with a useful assessment of the risk to avifauna from a wind farm development is to collect observational data on birds on site and to model the collision risk.  Regulators, in general, have accepted the collision risk model, as a sound scientific basis upon which to derive an assessment and to develop ensuing permit conditions for approval.  Such a model was developed by one of Australia’s leading avifauna consultants - Biosis Research Pty Ltd (Biosis Research) - for the Woolnorth wind farm. This is a “deterministic” model, which uses known, fixed values as inputs in order to provide an output that is a defined number (contingent of course upon the many assumptions made to construct the model).  This model has been subsequently modified and used at a number of other sites and by other wind farm proponents in Australia.

Hydro Tasmania has engaged Biosis Research to collect avian data, develop and run a collision risk model, and assess the outputs from the model for all of its Tasmanian wind farm developments – planned and existing.  Biosis Research has high credibility in the industry and has been used by assessment panels to provide expert advice on avifauna issues.

## **Identification of the Computational Error**

As part of the assessment of the proposed Heemskirk wind farm, the federal Department of Environment and Heritage (DEH) requested that a “stochastic” model be developed to estimate the impact of the development on Orange-bellied Parrots (OBPs).   Simplistically, a stochastic model replaces some or all of the fixed inputs to a deterministic model with a probability distribution or range of values for that particular input in order to quantify the likelihood or probability of any particular scenario.

During the course of developing the stochastic model for OBPs for the Heemskirk Wind Farm, Biosis Research discovered a computational flaw that predominantly relates to directionality of bird movements in relation to wind turbines.

As a consequence, a thorough review of the model was undertaken when the directionality flaw was identified, and in addition to the correction of the flaw, a number of refinements were made to the model to improve its validity and quality.  The other refinements are as follows:

- A more accurate method of calculating the number of turbines a bird could potentially collide with, in order to provide a realistic assessment of turbines encountered during any particular flight path.

- Application of population sizes to provide an estimate of the _individuals_ at risk, as opposed to the _movements_ at risk, in order to assess the potential impact to any species.

- Adjustment of the way in which bird observations from different points and times are combined, in order to provide a valid method of summing different observations.

- A refinement of the classes of birds modelled, in order to better represent different types of birds present on site.

- The application of separate avoidance rates for stationary and moving parts of the turbines.

- The use of the observed flight height of bird movements as opposed to the previously used pre-determined ratio of bird movements of 50:50 above and below rotor height, in order to be consistent with an ecologically reasonable model.

The use of the ‘Ecologically Reasonable’ model, which was presented in the Development Proposal and Environmental Management Plans (DPEMPs) for the Musselroe and Heemskirk wind farms, has been refined and the results using a revised Ecologically Reasonable Model (ERM) are presented in this report. A more complete description of the previous and revised ERM is described in the body of this revised assessment report.  This approach is derived from the study of the range of avoidance rates found in empirical research presented in international literature and recent Australian validation projects.  Results for a range of avoidance rates are presented in full in the Appendices to this report.

The details of the computational error, and the associated model correction, as well as other refinements, are explained in more detail in this report.

## **Key results**

Biosis Research has produced revised results for all bird collision risk modelling previously conducted for Hydro Tasmania’s wind farm developments. The deterministic model has been applied to all species for these projects, with the exception of Orange-bellied Parrots at the Heemskirk site, which have been modelled using the stochastic model.

A summary of revised results compared to previous results (estimated mortalities per annum for priority species) is provided in Table 0.1 below. The number of decimal places used varies, and relates to the species being examined (and the importance of the data resolution).

The results from the latest modelling show that only a very low number of birds are at risk of collision, with estimated collision rates for some species decreasing, some increasing and some staying the same. While there are some increases in estimated mortality, the revised estimated mortality rates do not represent a significant impact for any species.

## Validation of the model

The results from the revised model have been compared to actual results from dead bird searches conducted at two wind farms, in order to determine if estimations are similar to actual impacts. Dead bird searches have been conducted at the Woolnorth wind farm (stage 1) and the Codrington wind farm. At both of these sites, although dead bird monitoring has been intensive, the period of monitoring is relatively short and the number of dead birds detected is low, resulting in insufficient data to validate

the model for individual species. However, validation is possible when all species are combined.

The analysis reveals that mortality rates are consistent with the model estimations when an average avoidance rate of 99% is used, and that use of a lower avoidance rate overestimates risk.  Accordingly, the Ecologically Reasonable Model is considered a suitable basis for assessment, except in the specific case of waders where there is some uncertainty about bird movements at night. In this instance the use of a more conservative model is appropriate until further data are available.

## Proposed Mitigation

Proposed mitigation measures have been strengthened for priority species where the revised modelling has shown an increase in estimated mortality rate.  As stated above, the revised impact assessment predicts that the wind farm will not significantly impact any bird populations (as was the case with the original estimations) and therefore the mitigation measures proposed are considered valid and appropriate.

## Eagles

Hydro Tasmania recognises that protection of nests is a valid mitigation measure for managing impacts to eagles.  Hydro Tasmania has increased the commitment to the number of nests to be protected commensurate with the increase in the estimated level of impact on the populations of eagles.  Hydro Tasmania considers that the nest protection activities that are proposed as part of the Musselroe Wind Farm proposal are appropriate as mitigation measures to address the potential impacts to individual birds, which are low in comparison to the total population.

## Waders

The revised model estimates an equivalent level of impact to that estimated by the original model. At estimated mortality levels there will be no significant impact to any wader species. Although estimated mortality rates were low, Hydro Tasmania previously proposed to trial an automatic crepuscular turbine shutdown during periods when waders are present on site. However, additional information and assessment is provided that indicates that at the estimated low mortality levels a crepuscular shutdown is not warranted and the effectiveness of this measure cannot be tested. Therefore, Hydro has revised this proposal to trial the crepuscular shutdown in the event that mortalities exceed estimated levels and have potential for a significant impact on any affected species.

## Conclusion

The detection of the computational error within the model has been addressed by a thorough and extensive review of the model.  In addition to the correction of the error, the review has led to other refinements, and the outcome is a much more robust and mathematically valid model.

For the Musselroe wind farm the revised model for the majority of species show little or no change to previous model estimations and consequently indicate no greater risk of mortality than was previously considered.  The exceptions are with Wedge-tailed Eagles and White-bellied Sea-eagles, however the estimated risk from the revised modelling still does not constitute a significant impact to these species.

These results indicate that the project is not expected to significantly impact on any species, as demonstrated in this revised assessment report by comparisons with the populations of each species.  Further, Hydro Tasmania believes that the revised mitigation actions planned are commensurate with the estimated impact of the wind farms on any threatened species.

On the basis of this work, and preceding submissions, we believe that the project is now ready to be assessed and we remain confident that the projects are sustainable and pose no threat to ongoing viability of any species.

## **1 INTRODUCTION**

Hydro Tasmania has a large and comprehensive development strategy for wind farms in Australia, particularly in Tasmania where significant developments are underway, or are in the planning stage. Hydro Tasmania has received approval for the development of a wind farm in north-western Tasmania (the Woolnorth wind farm) and has just commissioned Stage 2 of this development (which takes the total number of turbines to 37).  Hydro Tasmania expects to develop the third and final stage in the short-medium term, and will seek approval to use Vestas V80 or V90 wind turbines at this site, rather than the V66 turbines for which approval was granted.  Further, Hydro Tasmania has submitted development applications for two new wind farms, Musselroe in the northeast of the state, and Heemskirk on the west coast of Tasmania. Avian collision risk modelling has been undertaken at each of these sites in order to determine the potential collision risk these developments pose to birds.

## **1.1 Background**

As part of the Woolnorth wind farm Development Application, Biosis Research developed an avian collision risk model that estimated the potential risk of birds colliding with wind turbines. The model required detailed data on the number and movements of birds on site, and the specifics of the wind turbines to estimate the potential rate of bird collisions with wind turbines per year.  This model is a deterministic model as it uses fixed values for the input variables, rather than random variables, and hence does not give any information about the variability of the results.  The deterministic model has been further developed since its use for the Woolnorth wind farm, and has been subsequently used to estimate the risk to birds at a number of proposed wind farms, including the Musselroe and Heemskirk wind farms.

As part of the Heemskirk wind farm proposal, the Department of Environment and Heritage (DEH) requested that the potential risk of the development to Orange-bellied Parrots Neophema chrysogaster (OBPs) be assessed using a stochastic model, that is one that incorporates variability in the input data. The stochastic model replaces a number of the deterministic variables with stochastic variables.  This allows a particular variable to be input as a probability distribution in order to provide a measure of variability in the outputs (a range of outcomes instead of a single value).  At Hydro Tasmania’s request Biosis Research developed a stochastic model in conjunction with Dr Michael McCarthy of the Australian Research Centre for Urban Ecology of the Royal Botanic Gardens Melbourne.

## **1.2 Identification of the error in the models**

While developing the stochastic model for OBPs at the Heemskirk wind farm, an error was found in the spreadsheets used to calculate the final results of both the deterministic and stochastic models.  The error related to the way in which the bird flight direction

was combined with the direction the wind turbines were facing.  This error meant that previous results had generally underestimated the collision risk.  Hydro Tasmania immediately informed DEH, Tasmanian Department of Primary Industry Water and Environment (DPIWE) and the Environmental Management and Pollution Control Board (the Board) of the error, and further assessment of the proposed Musselroe and Heemskirk wind farms was postponed until the error was resolved.

This computational error was rectified, but in order to determine that no other errors existed, a detailed review of the models was undertaken by Biosis Research and Hydro Tasmania.  Further refinements were made to the deterministic model to improve the representation of the interaction between birds and wind turbines.

This document provides information on the error correction and the refinements made to the model.  Revised estimations of avian collision risk for priority bird species are documented and proposed mitigation measures are revised in line with updated information.
